add.proof:
\emph{Heavy stacks.}
For the lattice argument assume (P3).
Basis extension gives $B^\top\mathbb Z^I=\mathbb Z^d$ for a saturated lattice.
The rank $d$ bound gives $m(\Theta)\le g^{-d}$.
If $\Pr[F]\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, then $m(F^\perp)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by the containing fiber.
Condition (I5) gives $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}>g^{-4}$.
Thus its normal lattice has rank at most three.

\emph{Prefix estimates.}

For a saturated rank $d$ lattice on $I$ with basis $B$, put the rows of a largest minor $J$ first.
Let $I_k$ be the first $k$ indices.
Let $\Theta_k$ be the integer points in the column span of $B_{I_k}$, with height $h_k$ and density $m_k$.
Invertibility gives $\Theta_d=\mathbb Z^J$. Its height is one. Point fibers give $m_d=g^{-d}$.
Saturation gives $\Theta_{|I|}=\Theta$.
For $d\le k\le |I|$ write $B_{I_k}=YC$ with $Y$ a basis matrix of $\Theta_k$ and $C$ a nonsingular integer matrix.
The maximal minors of $B_{I_k}$ scale those of $Y$ by $\det C$.
Thus $J$ remains a largest minor.
The fibers of $\Theta_k$ are the level sets of $B_{I_k}^\top$ because $C$ is invertible.
The image $G_k:=B_{I_k}^\top\mathbb Z^{I_k}$ is $C^\top\mathbb Z^d$ by saturation.
This image has index $|\det C|$.
The minor scaling thus gives $h_k[\mathbb Z^d:G_k]=h(\Theta)$.
Let $s_k$ be the order of the new row modulo $G_k$.
Adjoining the row enlarges $G_k$ by index $s_k$.
The height identity then gives $h_{k+1}=s_k h_k$.
The fiber value modulo $G_k$ fixes the new coordinate modulo the row order $s_k$.
There are at most $\lceil g/s_k\rceil$ such values in the box.
Conditioning on that coordinate gives $m_{k+1}\le m_k\lceil g/s_k\rceil/g$.
For $s_k\ge2$, $\lceil g/s_k\rceil/g\le1/s_k+1/g$.
$s^{1/b}-1-s/g$ is concave.
Its value at $g$ is nonnegative by $g\ge2^b$.
The exponential bound gives $2^{1/b}-1\ge(\ln2)/b$.
For $b\ge7$, $(\ln2)/b>2^{1-b}$.
Also $2^{1-b}\ge2/g$ by (I1).
Thus the function is positive at $2$.
Concavity gives $1+s_k/g\le s_k^{1/b}$ on $2\le s_k\le g$.
For $s_k=1$ the density ratio bound is one.
Multiplying gives $m_{k+1}^{b/(b-1)}h_{k+1}\le m_k^{b/(b-1)}h_k$ for $s_k<g$.

In rank three let $n'$ count the steps with $s_k\ge2$.
The density bound gives $g^3 m(\Theta)\le\prod_{s_k\ge2}(1/s_k+1/g)$.
The product of the $s_k$ is $h(\Theta)$.
The excess over $1/h(\Theta)$ is zero if $n'=0$.
Pairing subsets that differ at one fixed index gives $\binom{n'}j\le2^{n'-1}$ if $n'\ge1$.
By $1/s_k\le1/2$, the degree-$j$ excess is at most $2^{j-1}/g^j$ for $j\ge1$.
Summing bounds the excess by $1/(g-2)$.
Condition (I1) gives $1/(g-2)\le(1+3/g)/g$.
Bernoulli gives $\xi_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1+3/g$.
The product estimate gives $g^3m(\Theta)\le1/h(\Theta)+\xi_{\mathrm{tr}}/g$.
If $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, (I2) gives $h(\Theta)\le H_3/\xi_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Thus $g^3m(\Theta)h(\Theta)\le1+H_3/g$.
This implies regularity by (I4).

\emph{Counting trimmed images.}
Take $F$ on $I\cup\{i'\}$ trimmed by a rank $d$ lattice $\Theta$ on $I$.
Fibers of $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_I,r_{i'})$ have density at most $m(\Theta)/g$ by independence.
For full image dimension $k=d+1$ in a coset of index $q$, retain all coordinates.
In the other case assume $F^\perp$ has rank $1\le d'<d$, with a largest minor at $J\subseteq I$, and its restrictions to $I$ lie in the span of $\Theta$.
Put $k=d+1-d'$.
The rows $B_J$ have rank $d'$ since their column span contains the invertible minor of a basis of $F^\perp$.
Choose the final $k-1$ columns $B_2$ of $B$ to vanish on $J$, by extending an integer basis of the saturated kernel of $B_J$ to an integer basis of $\mathbb Z^d$.
The shape formula gives $12 B(B^\top B)^{-1}B^\top/g^2$ as the ellipsoid form on centered $r_I$.
The orthogonal projector depends only on the column span.
Fibers depend only on that span.
Height is invariant by unimodularity.
Write $B_1$ for the other columns.
The pullback $a\mapsto(Ba_{[d]},a_{d+1})$ is injective by full column rank of $B$. It maps image normals onto the normals of $F$ by the restriction hypothesis.
Thus the image has affine dimension $k$.
If $V$ is a basis matrix of $\Phi(F)^\perp$, split it into row blocks $V_1,V_2,V_3$ with $d',k-1,1$ rows.
The mapped basis generates a full-rank sublattice of $F^\perp$. Its minor at $J$ gives $|\det(B_1)_J|\,|\det V_1|\ge h(F^\perp)$.
The inequality makes $V_1$ invertible. Dropping the first $d'$ coordinates is injective because differences satisfy $V^\top y=0$.
Write $(y_2,x)$ for the retained coordinates, with $x$ last. Projected differences vanish under $(y_2,x)\mapsto V_2^\top y_2+V_3^\top x$ modulo $V_1^\top\mathbb Z^{d'}$.
Normal-lattice saturation gives surjectivity.
The projected coset has index $|\det V_1|$.
Let $\delta$ be the retained coset index.

Use $B_2=B$ with empty $J$ and $B_1$ in full dimension.
The empty minor has determinant one.
The projected unit ball fits in the cube of side two.
The projection formula gives volume at most $g(T_{\mathrm{tr}}/\sqrt N)^{k-1}\sqrt{\det(B_2^\top B_2)}$ for interval length at most $g$.
The image contains a simplex of volume at least $\delta/k!$ by the coset determinant.
An affine map of the coset to $\mathbb Z^k$ divides volumes by $\delta$.
Blichfeldt bounds the convex cylinder count by $k!$ times scaled volume plus $k$.
The simplex bound absorbs $k$ into $(k+1)!$ times the scaled volume.
Since $(B_2)_J=0$, multiplying its complementary-row minors by $\det(B_1)_J$ gives minors of $B$ up to sign.
There are at most $N^{k-1}$ such minors.
Cauchy--Binet therefore gives $|\det(B_1)_J|\sqrt{\det(B_2^\top B_2)}\le h(\Theta)N^{(k-1)/2}$.
For $k-1=1,2,3$, (I3) gives $(k+1)!T_{\mathrm{tr}}^{k-1}\le g^{k-1}\Lambda_{k-1}$.
The count times fiber density gives $\Pr[F]\,\delta|\det(B_1)_J|\le g^{k-1}\Lambda_{k-1}h(\Theta)m(\Theta)$.
In full dimension $\delta|\det(B_1)_J|=q$.
The normal minor gives $\delta|\det(B_1)_J|\ge h(F^\perp)$ otherwise.

\emph{Regularizing a dense lattice.}
Take a saturated rank $d$ lattice of density at least $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$. We seek a regular saturated superlattice losing at most $(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ in density.
Induct downwards from rank three, where the prefix estimate already gives regularity.
For $d<3$ use the prefix order with largest minor first.
The prefix densities are nonincreasing by the density recursion.
Take successively a densest prefix fiber $F_k$, trimming it by $\tilde\Theta_{k-1}$ if the preceding normal lattice exceeded the preceding prefix.
Trimming gives $\Pr[F_k]\ge m_k-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If $F_k^\perp$ exceeds $\Theta_k$, its rank is at least $d+1$ by saturation.
Its rank is at most three by the density bound.
Its density meets the induction threshold $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-\operatorname{rank}F_k^\perp)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by $m_k\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The induction gives a regular superlattice $\tilde\Theta_k$ with density at least $m_k-(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If $F_{|I|}^\perp\ne\Theta$, use its regular superlattice.

Otherwise let $j$ be the last promoted prefix, or $d-1$ if none was promoted.
For $j<k<|I|$, if $s_k\ge g$ then the next coordinate is constant on $F_{k+1}$.
Its unit vector then belongs to $F_{k+1}^\perp=\Theta_{k+1}$.
It vanishes on $J$, contradicting invertibility.
Thus $s_k<g$.
The prefix estimate bounds $m(\Theta)^{b/(b-1)}h(\Theta)$ by $m_{j+1}^{b/(b-1)}h_{j+1}$.
Since $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, a bound of $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}^{1/(b-1)}\Gamma_d/g^d$ suffices.
If $j=d-1$, this is the initial height and density bound together with (I4).
Otherwise let $\tilde d$ be the rank of $\tilde\Theta_j$.
The normal lattice of $F_{j+1}$ is $\Theta_{j+1}$, with largest minor at $J$.
Its restriction lies in the span of $\Theta_j\subseteq\tilde\Theta_j$.
Thus the lower-dimensional estimate applies to $F_{j+1}$ trimmed by $\tilde\Theta_j$.
By regularity of $\tilde\Theta_j$ the estimate gives $\Pr[F_{j+1}]h_{j+1}\le\Lambda_{\tilde d-d}\Gamma_{\tilde d}/g^d$.
The trimming bound and (I4) give $m_{j+1}\le A_{\mathrm{inv}}\Pr[F_{j+1}]$ for $m_{j+1}\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

Monotonicity and trimming give $m_{j+1}\le\Pr[F_j]+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The promoted normal rank gives $\Pr[F_j]\le g^{-d-1}$.
Now (I4) gives $m_{j+1}^{1/(b-1)}\le\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}^{1/(b-1)}P_d$.
Multiplying gives $m_{j+1}^{b/(b-1)}h_{j+1}\le\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}^{1/(b-1)}A_{\mathrm{inv}}\Lambda_{\tilde d-d}\Gamma_{\tilde d}P_d/g^d$.
This gives the required bound by (I4).
Thus the original lattice is regular in this case.

\emph{The modular fiber.}

For a nonzero $v$ with $v_0=0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$, omit coordinate zero and the zero entries to obtain $v_1,\ldots,v_{N_0}$.
Conditioning on the coordinates after a prefix bounds the full guessing probability by that of the prefix.
We inductively find a regular saturated lattice $\Theta$ of density $m(\Theta)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ whose reduction contains $v_{[i]}$.
For $i=1$, use $\mathbb Z$, whose density $1/g$ is that of the densest modular fiber by injectivity on the box.
Its density above $\theta$ implies $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}<1/g$.
Now $\Gamma_1\ge1$ follows from (I4).
Thus the initial lattice of height one is regular.
Regularity bounds the induction lattice's height by $H_d$ for $d\le2$.
The rank-three estimate gives the bound $H_3$ otherwise.

Restriction to a largest minor $J$ gives a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)$.
The cited successive minima and basis bound on this lattice gives a basis there with product of $\ell_1$ norms at most $h(\Theta)$, $2h(\Theta)$ or $9h(\Theta)$ in ranks one, two or three.
Lift this basis to the columns of $B$.
For a span vector $y$, Cramer's rule expresses $y_i$ linearly in $y_J$ by minor ratios.
Maximality makes each magnitude at most one.
The triangle inequality gives $\|y\|_\infty\le\|y_J\|_1$.

Write $v_{[i]}=Bc'$ modulo $q$.
For the next prefix take a densest modular fiber trimmed by $\Theta$, denoted by $F$.
Trimming gives $\Pr[F]>\theta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
In particular $\Pr[F]>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Under $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_{[i]},r_{i+1})$ the image satisfies a congruence with coefficients $c=(c',v_{i+1})$.
The coset has index $q$ because $v_{i+1}\ne0$.
In full dimension the trimmed image bound gives $\Pr[F]\le\Lambda_dg^dh(\Theta)m(\Theta)/q$.
Regularity bounds this by $\Lambda_d\Gamma_d/q$.
Condition (I5) makes this smaller than $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Thus the affine dimension is at most $d$.
Let $\Delta$ be the matrix of differences of image points.
The trimming ellipsoid's coordinate width bounds row $j\le d$ of $\Delta$ by $2R_{\mathrm{tr}}\sqrt{e_j^\top\Sigma_\Theta e_j}$.
The shape formula bounds this by $T_{\mathrm{tr}}\|Be_j\|_\infty$.
Last-row differences are at most $g-1$.
This is below $T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by $R_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge20$.
The determinant expansion bounds its nonzero maximal minors by $d!T_{\mathrm{tr}}^d\prod_j\|Be_j\|_\infty$, since the rank is at most $d$ and each row bound is at least one.
This is below $q$ by the basis and height bounds and (I5).
A nonzero maximal minor below $q$ preserves the rank of $\Delta$ modulo $q$.
The integer left kernel is saturated by torsion-freeness. Basis extension keeps its rank mod $q$.
Rank-nullity gives that rank to the modular left kernel.
The two spaces are therefore equal by containment.
Lift $c$ to $u$ in the integer left kernel.
Then $(Bu_{[d]},u_{d+1})$ belongs to $F^\perp$, by pulling the constant functional on $\Phi(F)$ back through $\Phi$.
Its reduction is $v_{[i+1]}$.
Its normal rank is at most three by the density bound.
Its rank is positive since it contains a lift of $v_{[i+1]}$.
By the definition of $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $m(F^\perp)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Regularization gives a superlattice with loss at most $2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
It contains the lift.

Choose $z_0\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $Bz_0\equiv v_{[N_0]}\bmod q$.
The line spanned by its nonzero residue has preimage of index $q^{d-1}$.
Restriction to a largest minor $J$ makes its determinant $h(\Theta)q^{d-1}$.
By (I6) this is at most $\beta^d/d!$, using $\lfloor H_3\rfloor$ in rank three.
The closed $\ell_1$ ball of radius $\beta$ has volume $(2\beta)^d/d!$.
Minkowski gives a nonzero $B_Jz$ in this ball.
The largest-minor bound gives $\|Bz\|_\infty\le\beta$.
The nonzero subvector $B_Jz$ gives $Bz$ nonzero residue since $\beta<q$.
That residue is a multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$ by the lattice choice.
Restore the zero coordinates to obtain $x$.

\emph{Application to heavy stacks.}

For heavy $\mathbf W$, choose a column basis including column zero if nonzero.
Condition only on $[N]$ entries outside the basis.
Each fiber fixes at most one basis tuple.
The independent sampler entries have $g$ equiprobable residues since $g+1<q$.
When zero is absent the stack ignores $r_0$.
Conditioning and the positive basis entries fix $r_0-r_\star$.
Thus a required $r_0$ residue specifies $r_\star$.
The required tuple has probability at most $g^{-\operatorname{rank}\mathbf W}$.
For rank at least four this is at most $g^{-4}$.
That contradicts heaviness since $g^{-4}<\theta$.
Each stack fiber lies in a fiber of $v^\top$ by row-space membership.
Thus $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$.
A kernel vector satisfies $v_0=0$ by the form $\varphi_0$.
The modular fiber argument above supplies its short multiple under (P3).
Any short multiple reduces to a nonzero vector in the kernel, by linearity.
Its coordinate zero is zero as an integer by $\beta<q$.
The form definitions identify the remaining forms with coefficients of $A\hat x$.
The coefficient list of $\hat x$ is $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ padded with zeros.
Its norm is therefore the positive norm of $x$.
\emph{Witness in the row space.}
First take a nonzero usable stack with row space $\mathcal V$ of dimension at most three and no kernel vector. Let $\mathcal U$ have columns a basis of $\mathcal V$, with rows $u_i$.
Let $d$ count the basis columns.
Form $h_s=\mathcal U^\top\sigma^s(z)$ for every integer $s$.
The coordinates of $h_0$ are independent over $\mathbb F_q$ since $z$ has zero kernel on $\mathcal V$.
The entries of $h_{n/2-1}$ remain base-field independent under Frobenius. Its first $d$ consecutive conjugates form an invertible Moore matrix.
Apply a left inverse of $\mathcal U$ on the left and its transpose on the right of $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ to obtain $\Xi_s$ at $s=n/2-1,n/2,n/2+1$, respectively. Congruence preserves symmetry.
Multiplication by $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal U^\top$ recovers each matrix by its column and row spaces.
Reduction modulo $P$ writes the ties using the three conjugations because $\omega^{n/2}=-1$.
Applying the left inverse gives their equations $\Xi_s h_{s'}=\Xi_{s'}h_s$.
If $\sum_s\varrho_s h_s=0$, the matrix $\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s$ kills each $h_{s'}$ by the ties.
It is therefore zero by spanning.
Thus there is a linear map $\Xi(h_s)=\Xi_s$.
The form $\Xi(h;u,u')=u^\top\Xi(h)u'$ is symmetric in $u,u'$ by symmetry of the matrices.
The ties give symmetry in $h,u'$ by spanning.
The cellwise Booleanity tests extend linearly to the three matrices.
In coordinates they give $\Xi(h_s;u_j,u_j-u_0)=0$.
Spanning extends this to every $h$.
The even powers of $W_V$ make it fixed by $\sigma^{n/2}$.
Consequently $\Xi_{n/2}=\sigma^{n/2}(\Xi_{n/2})$.
Also $\Xi_{n/2-1}=\sigma^{n/2-1}(\Xi_{n/2+1})$ because the two exponents add to $n$.

The tensor is nonzero because $W_U,W_V$ determine the stack.
If $u_0=0$, take basis rows of $\mathcal U$.
All repeated entries vanish by Booleanity and symmetry.
A nonzero entry requires $d=3$.
Symmetry leaves one nonzero value $t$ on distinct basis rows.
The off-diagonal conjugate identities give $t h_s=\sigma^s(t)h_0$ for $s=n/2-1,n/2$.
Both conjugates are multiples of $h_0$ because $t\ne0$.
This contradicts the Moore basis.

Extend $u_0$ to a basis of rows at indices $J$.
For $\delta\in\{0,1\}^{J\setminus\{0\}}$, choose $p_\delta$ with $u_0^\top p_\delta=1$ and $u_j^\top p_\delta=\delta_j$ at the other basis indices.
Booleanity permits replacing a repeated nonzero index by zero.
Symmetry then leaves one entry for each nonzero index set $A$ in a triple.
The cubes give the subset incidence entries $\prod_{k\in A}\delta_k$.
Ordering subsets by size gives a triangular matrix with unit diagonal.
Hence $\Xi(h)=\sum_\delta c_\delta(h^\top p_\delta)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
Every $A$ also occurs in a pair for $d\le3$.
The same triangular matrix gives independence of the squares.
Form $w_\delta=\mathcal U p_\delta$.
Then $z(w_\delta)\ne0$ by the kernel hypothesis.
Comparing square coefficients shows that both conjugations fix $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)$.
Their consecutive powers generate $\sigma$.
Thus $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)\in\mathbb F_q$.

Fix $c_\delta\ne0$, which exists since the tensor is nonzero.
For a passing test $\varrho$, put $\mathcal Q=\sum_\delta\frac{c_\delta}{z(w_\delta)}\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
The test vanishes on $W_U$ and $W_V$ by linearity on the cells.
It vanishes on $\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ by base-field linearity under conjugation.
Substitution gives $h_0^\top\mathcal Qh_s=0$ for the three conjugate indices.
Spanning gives $h_0^\top\mathcal Q=0$.
The field independence of the coordinates of $h_0$ gives $\mathcal Q=0$, since $\mathcal Q$ has base-field entries.
Square independence gives $\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)=0$ for this nonzero coefficient.
Booleanity gives $(w_\delta)_j((w_\delta)_j-1)=0$ for $j\in[N]$.
Each constraint test on $w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ gives its constraint on $w_\delta$ by substitution into the test.
Since $(w_\delta)_0=1$, this is a witness in $\mathcal V$.

\emph{The extractor tests.}

Each candidate is checked against $S$ before output.
Pairing multiplies input coefficients by its expression rule.
The resulting cell matrix is the outer product of the two coefficient vectors by the cell definition.
Applying the probes to that matrix gives the specified record update.
Up to the first mark, records represent monitor entries with guess variables set to zero, up to formal equality.
Indeed an unseen valid operand is a guess, represented by zero.
The substitution of zero commutes with the operations on expressions.
The monitor keeps only formally equal expressions at a label before the first mark.
The view result for a formally zero difference gives $W_c r=u_c$ at every $r$.
Varying $r$ forces each $W_c$ to vanish.
Thus formally equal expressions have equal stacks.

The coefficients of $G_T$ and $\mathsf K^\alpha$ give zero stacks.
At a good key mark the entry has no guess variable by (M4).
Its nonzero stack therefore identifies it as a result.
Hence its sketches are tested.
At a good difference mark, the old entry has a record by the time the result is tested.
Indeed, a guess that has never been an answered operand cannot cancel from the difference unless it is an operand of the current call.
Thus the tested difference has the mark stack, by linearity and the record invariant.

Fix a run with a good first mark and no kernel vector in the mark row space.
Its stack is usable by the view result. Its row space has dimension at most three by the rank bound just proved.
Symmetry makes the image of $(v_c)_c\mapsto\sum_c W_c v_c$ the row space.
Conditional on the run, the independent probes give three independent uniform images in the row space.
Their span equals the row space except with probability at most $2/q$.
That row space contains a witness by the preceding tied-form argument.
Coordinate zero is a pivot since the witness has a nonzero entry there.
The witness is among the candidates by its Boolean entries.
If extraction has not succeeded earlier, the test is reached.
Averaging over runs proves the probability bound.

\emph{Lifting.}
Take a kernel vector $v$ as in (R5).
Drop coordinate zero.
Put a nonzero coordinate first.
Scale to set $v_1=1$.
Use integer vectors of norm at most $\beta$ in each prefix whose residues are on the prefix line of $v$.
Each column is a multiple of a fixed integer lift of the prefix of $v$ plus a $q$-divisible column.
Multilinearity makes every four-row minor divisible by $q^3$ since terms with two lift columns vanish.
Its magnitude is at most $24\beta^4$ by determinant expansion.
It vanishes by (P4).
Thus each prefix span has dimension at most three.

Start with the basis $1$, feasible by (I6).
A nonzero bounded vector has nonzero residue by $\beta<q$.
On the line its first residue is nonzero since $v_1=1$.
Thus its prefixes are nonzero.
Return $\bot$ on a zero prefix span.

A bounded extension has its prefix in the stored span by induction.
Let $B$ have the $d$ stored basis columns at prefix $i$.
The extension map is $(z,x_{i+1})\mapsto(Bz,x_{i+1})$.
Use integer representatives of $v$ in $[0,q)$.
For $j\le i$ use the rows of $(Bz)_j-(Bz)_1v_j$.
For the new entry use the row of $x_{i+1}-(Bz)_1v_{i+1}$.
Add the row of $q(Bz)_1$.
An integral line extension gives pairings in $q\mathbb Z$.
Conversely these pairings force integral $x_1$ and each difference in $q\mathbb Z$.
Common zeros of the forms map to zero.
The extension map is injective by column independence.
Thus the row lattice has full rank.
Hermite reduction gives its basis.
Multiplying its inverse transpose by $q$ gives the lattice of parameters with pairings in $q\mathbb Z$.
Express the coordinate bounds as linear inequalities on its at most four integer coefficients.
Take integer functionals spanning the annihilator of the previously found solutions in these coordinates.
An outside vector meets threshold one for some signed functional.
Fixed-dimensional integer programming does these tests in polynomial time.
At most four rounds find a basis of all bounded solutions.
Store those vectors for the next step.
The row formulas bound entries by $\beta q$. Their bit lengths are $O(\log q)$ since $\beta<q$.
Hermite reduction keeps polynomial bit lengths. Fixed-size inversion preserves them.

Return any nonzero final vector, or $\bot$ if none exists.
Undo the permutation and restore coordinate zero.

\emph{The reductions.}
Uniform challenges give jointly uniform programmed entries. (R1) samples other entries independently.
Exchangeability of unused labels and exponents gives uniform injections.
Thus (R1) has the law of the run with message $m_b$.
Independence allows sampling (R2) before (R1).

At a good key mark, (R3) takes the target record.
It represents $\mathsf D$ up to formal equality by the record invariant.
At a good difference mark, the analogous record difference represents $\mathsf D$.
By the invariant, earlier equal-label records are formally equal.
Thus no earlier difference is detected.
In the difference case $\mathsf D$ is formally nonzero by (M3).
The degree bound applies to $\varpi\operatorname{val}(\mathsf D)$.
On valid coins $\varpi\ne0$ by its factors.
This polynomial is nonzero since $\mathsf D$ is formally nonzero.
The coordinate $\tau$ excludes $D$ values.
The coordinate $\varepsilon$ excludes at most $K_1+1$ values.
The grid gives $K_1<n$. Thus at most $D$ are excluded by (P1).
Every other coin excludes at most one value.
Schwartz--Zippel bounds private evaluation failure by $d_f/(q-D)\le\varepsilon_f$.

By encryption, $\kappa$ is independent of $r,\alpha$.
For fixed valid coins other than $\alpha$, the good-mark affine identity holds at two $\alpha$ values.
The constant term gives the plain identity $\chi\kappa$ at $r$.
The linear term gives $-\mathsf D_K\kappa$ for the alpha pairs without the copy factor.
These values are affine in $r$ by the right exponent formulas.
The view locus makes each value constant on its sector's stack fiber.
Its gradient thus annihilates that stack's kernel.
The gradient lies in the row space by duality.
In particular the plain gradient vanishes when the mark uses the alpha sector.
Formal equality gives equal affine functions of $r$. Hence their derivatives agree.

For each point, keep $\pi,s_{\mathrm X},\upsilon,y,\varepsilon,\Omega_{12},\zeta''$ random and fix the other coins.
Only the first right coordinates contain $r$ by the published formulas.
Their derivatives after removing the sector factor have the single coefficient $s_{\mathrm{leg}}$.
A second left factor's term in $y_i$ contains $\Omega_{12}$.
The cancellation column has $\zeta''$ instead of $\pi$.
The constant part of $1+\varepsilon\omega^{2k_1}$ is one.
Dividing $\lfloor k_c/2\rfloor$ by $K_1$ gives remainder $k_1$ and quotient $k_2$.
In the sector gradient after removing the common sector factor, the coefficient of $\pi s_{\mathrm X}\upsilon^{k_c}y_i$ is the row $W_{c,i}$.
The cell and leg indices bound each $\upsilon$ exponent by $n-1$.
Outside $\upsilon$, a term uses at most one $s_{\mathrm X}$, at most one of $\pi,\zeta''$, and at most one each of $y_i,\varepsilon,\Omega_{12}$.
So the gradient has degree at most $n+4$.
Choose $d$ mark-stack basis rows. Project onto columns of a nonzero minor of those rows.
The determinant of the first $d$ projected vectors has this minor as the coefficient of the product of the selected monomials at the separate points.
Its degree is at most $d(n+4)$.
By $d\le3$ and $n\le D$, this is at most $d_f$.
Schwartz--Zippel therefore bounds span failure by $\varepsilon_f$.

On both successes, (R5) finds a kernel vector since the recovered row space is the mark row space.
The lattice argument supplies a short multiple.
The lifting algorithm returns one.
Packing gives an MSIS solution.
Any earlier successful output also solves MSIS because (R5) uses a kernel vector and a short multiple.
